claim: Thermal damage of the larval zebrafish fin disrupts collagen organization and wound healing compared to tail transection.
source: Previously we reported that thermal damage of the larval zebrafish fin disrupts collagen organization and wound healing compared to tail transection (LeBert et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (LeBert et al., 2018).

claim: Each damage model triggers distinct inflammatory and tissue responses.
source: We found that each damage model triggers distinct inflammatory and tissue responses, with Stat3 and TGFβ playing key roles in the regulation of mesenchymal cells during simple repair.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing different inflammatory and tissue responses across wound models.

claim: Stat3 and TGFβ play key roles in the regulation of mesenchymal cells during simple repair.
source: We found that each damage model triggers distinct inflammatory and tissue responses, with Stat3 and TGFβ playing key roles in the regulation of mesenchymal cells during simple repair.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of stat3 mutation and TGFβ inhibition on mesenchymal cells and wound healing.

claim: Thermal injury disrupts collagen fibers initially.
source: While thermal injury disrupts collagen fibers initially, healing is recovered as inflammation resolves, and mesenchymal cells and collagen fibers align.
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG microscopy data showing loss of collagen fibers after thermal injury.

claim: Healing is recovered as inflammation resolves following thermal injury.
source: While thermal injury disrupts collagen fibers initially, healing is recovered as inflammation resolves, and mesenchymal cells and collagen fibers align.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing tissue regrowth recovery by 96 hpw and temporal correlation with inflammation resolution.

claim: Mesenchymal cells and collagen fibers align as healing recovers from thermal injury.
source: While thermal injury disrupts collagen fibers initially, healing is recovered as inflammation resolves, and mesenchymal cells and collagen fibers align.
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG microscopy and vimentin reporter data showing fiber reappearance and organization.

claim: Infected wounds lead to persistent inflammation.
source: By contrast, infected wounds lead to persistent inflammation and loss of mesenchymal cells, resulting in minimal tissue repair.
evidence: This claim is supported by leukocyte recruitment data showing continued inflammation up to 168 hpw in infected wounds.

claim: Infected wounds lead to loss of mesenchymal cells.
source: By contrast, infected wounds lead to persistent inflammation and loss of mesenchymal cells, resulting in minimal tissue repair.
evidence: This claim is supported by vimentin reporter data showing progressive decline of vimGFP-positive cells in infected wounds.

claim: Infected wounds result in minimal tissue repair.
source: By contrast, infected wounds lead to persistent inflammation and loss of mesenchymal cells, resulting in minimal tissue repair.
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue regrowth area measurements showing significantly reduced healing in infected wounds.

claim: Caudal fin transection and sterile needle wounding of larval zebrafish are invaluable in vivo models of inflammation and wound repair.
source: Caudal fin transection or sterile needle wounding of larval zebrafish have become invaluable in vivo models of inflammation and wound repair (LeBert and Huttenlocher, 2014; Renshaw et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing these models.

claim: Zebrafish wound models have led to key insights into early wound signals.
source: These models have led to key insights into early wound signals (Niethammer et al., 2009; Yoo et al., 2012; Yoo et al., 2011) and mechanisms of resolution of inflammation (Mathias et al., 2006; Tauzin et al., 2014) due, in part, to the unique capability for monitoring the wound response over a long duration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on wound signals.

claim: Zebrafish wound models have led to key insights into mechanisms of resolution of inflammation.
source: These models have led to key insights into early wound signals (Niethammer et al., 2009; Yoo et al., 2012; Yoo et al., 2011) and mechanisms of resolution of inflammation (Mathias et al., 2006; Tauzin et al., 2014) due, in part, to the unique capability for monitoring the wound response over a long duration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on inflammation resolution.

claim: Sterile wounds are akin to controlled surgical wounds, lacking complexities associated with traumatic injuries or complications such as infections.
source: These sterile wounds are akin to controlled surgical wounds, lacking complexities associated with traumatic injuries or complications such as infections (Velnar et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and established knowledge about wound types.

claim: A burn wound assay was introduced to study the role of collagen-based epithelial projections during wound repair.
source: We recently introduced a burn wound assay that disrupts collagen organization to study the role of collagen-based epithelial projections during wound repair (LeBert et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Thermal injury at the caudal fin led to a dramatic loss of collagen fibers in the wound region.
source: We found that, unlike the simple transection, thermal injury at the caudal fin led to a dramatic loss of collagen fibers in the wound region, accompanied by a marked impact on healing progression at 48 hr post wound (hpw).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (LeBert et al., 2018) and data in the current manuscript.

claim: Thermal injury at the caudal fin had a marked impact on healing progression at 48 hr post wound.
source: We found that, unlike the simple transection, thermal injury at the caudal fin led to a dramatic loss of collagen fibers in the wound region, accompanied by a marked impact on healing progression at 48 hr post wound (hpw).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and data showing reduced tissue regrowth.

claim: Wound healing in the burn wound was attenuated between 24 and 72 hpw.
source: Wound healing in the burn wound was attenuated between 24 and 72 hpw, but unexpectedly recovered such that the tissue regrowth area was comparable to that of simple transection by 96 hpw (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue regrowth area measurements shown in Figure 1B,D.

claim: Tissue regrowth area in burn wounds was comparable to simple transection by 96 hpw.
source: Wound healing in the burn wound was attenuated between 24 and 72 hpw, but unexpectedly recovered such that the tissue regrowth area was comparable to that of simple transection by 96 hpw (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue regrowth area measurements shown in Figure 1B,D.

claim: Events leading up to 72 hpw were critical to facilitating the healing process in burn wounds.
source: This observation suggested that events leading up to 72 hpw were critical to facilitating the healing process.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that healing recovers after 72 hpw.

claim: Tissue regrowth area post Lm-infected transection remained markedly diminished relative to simple transection, even at 168 hpw.
source: The tissue regrowth area post Lm-infected transection remained markedly diminished relative to simple transection, even at 168 hpw (7 days post infection, dpi) (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue regrowth area measurements shown in Figure 1C,E.

claim: The infection had no measurable impact on the survival of larvae.
source: Importantly, the infection had no measurable impact on the survival of larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Bacteria entered at the wound site and expanded, peaking at 72–96 hpw.
source: We found that bacteria entered at the wound site and expanded, peaking at 72–96 hpw, and were largely cleared from the host by 120–168 hpw (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data of mCherry-expressing L. monocytogenes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Bacteria were largely cleared from the host by 120–168 hpw.
source: We found that bacteria entered at the wound site and expanded, peaking at 72–96 hpw, and were largely cleared from the host by 120–168 hpw (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing reduced bacterial signal at later timepoints.

claim: The infection remained localized in most cases.
source: Although the infection remained localized, limited dissemination of bacteria occurred in small patches along the neural tube (17 out of 47 larvae, three biological replicates) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing bacteria primarily at wound site.

claim: Limited dissemination of bacteria occurred in small patches along the neural tube in 17 out of 47 larvae.
source: Although the infection remained localized, limited dissemination of bacteria occurred in small patches along the neural tube (17 out of 47 larvae, three biological replicates) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data and quantification of dissemination.

claim: L. monocytogenes did not infect unwounded larvae.
source: L. monocytogenes did not infect unwounded larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing no bacterial signal in unwounded larvae.

claim: The burn wound recruited significantly more neutrophils and macrophages compared to simple transection.
source: Although the inflammation in the burn wound followed a similar trend as that in the simple transection, the burn wound recruited significantly more neutrophils and macrophages (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by leukocyte count data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Neutrophil recruitment peaked at different times in burn wound versus simple transection but appeared to resolve by 24 hpw in both conditions.
source: Interestingly, while neutrophil recruitment peaked at different times, it appeared to resolve by 24 hpw in both conditions (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by neutrophil count data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The number of macrophages reached peak levels at 6 hpw and were clearing by 96 hpw in both transection and burn injuries.
source: The number of macrophages reached peak levels at 6 hpw and were clearing by 96 hpw in both injuries (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by macrophage count data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Leukocyte infiltration at the wound site over time appeared to be related to wound repair.
source: The leukocyte infiltration at the wound site over time appeared to be related to wound repair, as we detected minimal recruitment at the caudal fin of age-matched unwounded larvae (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of wounded versus unwounded larvae shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: TNFα-positive macrophages are considered M1-like macrophages.
source: We considered TNFα-positive macrophages to be M1-like macrophages as previously reported (Nguyen-Chi et al., 2015), and TNFα-negative as a differentially activated macrophage population.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Nguyen-Chi et al., 2015).

claim: The response appeared to be more pro-inflammatory in the burn wound.
source: The response appeared to be more pro-inflammatory in the burn wound (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by TNFα expression data in macrophages shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: At least 50% of macrophages in the burn wound were TNFα-positive by 24 hpw.
source: While mostly TNFα-negative macrophages are recruited to a simple transection throughout the course of the wound response, the burn wound recruits a more polarized population of macrophages (Figure 2A,C), where at least 50% of macrophages in the burn wound were TNFα-positive by 24 hpw.
evidence: This claim is supported by TNFα expression data shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: TNFα-positive macrophages were most prominent 6–48 hpw in burn wounds and began to subside by 72 hpw.
source: There is also a shift in the proportion of differentially activated macrophages in the burn wound; TNFα-positive macrophages were most prominent 6–48 hpw and began to subside by 72 hpw, while the total number of macrophages was maintained over this time period (Figure 2C), and by 96 hpw most macrophages in the burn wound were TNFα-negative.
evidence: This claim is supported by TNFα expression data over time shown in Figure 2C.

claim: By 96 hpw most macrophages in the burn wound were TNFα-negative.
source: There is also a shift in the proportion of differentially activated macrophages in the burn wound; TNFα-positive macrophages were most prominent 6–48 hpw and began to subside by 72 hpw, while the total number of macrophages was maintained over this time period (Figure 2C), and by 96 hpw most macrophages in the burn wound were TNFα-negative.
evidence: This claim is supported by TNFα expression data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The shift in macrophage activation (72–96 hpw) appears to coincide with the time period when healing begins to recover in the burn wound.
source: Interestingly, this shift in macrophage activation (72–96 hpw) appears to coincide with the time period when healing begins to recover in the burn wound (72–96 hpw; Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from temporal correlation between macrophage activation shift and healing recovery.

claim: Macrophages undergo a phenotypic switch during the different phases of wound repair to support optimal healing.
source: This is consistent with evidence that macrophages undergo a phenotypic switch (switch from M1- to M2-like activation) during the different phases of wound repair to support optimal healing (Krzyszczyk et al., 2018; Novak and Koh, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on macrophage phenotypic switching.

claim: Both neutrophil and macrophage infiltration increased over time in Lm-infected transection.
source: Both neutrophil and macrophage infiltration increased over time, to the extent that we were not able to count individual leukocytes reliably beyond 48 hpw (Figure 2D–F; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by leukocyte recruitment data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: The majority of macrophages were TNFα-positive in infected tail wounds and the proportion remained similar throughout the time course.
source: Unlike in the simple transection, the majority of macrophages were TNFα-positive and the proportion remained similar throughout the time course at the infected tail wound (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by TNFα expression data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The inflammation began to clear by 168 hpw (7 dpi) in infected wounds.
source: The inflammation began to clear by 168 hpw (7 dpi) (Figure 2D,G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2F), suggesting that regenerate growth may recover beyond 168 hpw.
evidence: This claim is supported by leukocyte recruitment data showing reduced inflammation at 168 hpw.

claim: Regenerate growth may recover beyond 168 hpw in infected wounds.
source: The inflammation began to clear by 168 hpw (7 dpi) (Figure 2D,G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2F), suggesting that regenerate growth may recover beyond 168 hpw.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation that inflammation is clearing.

claim: The persistent presence of TNFα-positive macrophages appears to negatively correlate with wound repair.
source: Moreover, the persistent presence of TNFα-positive macrophages appears to negatively correlate with wound repair.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that infected wounds with persistent TNFα-positive macrophages show impaired healing.

claim: Proper collagen fiber organization is essential for functional wound repair in larval zebrafish.
source: Our previous work showed that proper collagen fiber organization is essential for functional wound repair in larval zebrafish (LeBert et al., 2015) and that induction of vimentin expression in cells at the wound edge plays an important role in collagen (I and II) production and fiber reorganization (LeBert et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (LeBert et al., 2015).

claim: Induction of vimentin expression in cells at the wound edge plays an important role in collagen (I and II) production and fiber reorganization.
source: Our previous work showed that proper collagen fiber organization is essential for functional wound repair in larval zebrafish (LeBert et al., 2015) and that induction of vimentin expression in cells at the wound edge plays an important role in collagen (I and II) production and fiber reorganization (LeBert et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (LeBert et al., 2018).

claim: Collagen fibers were completely disrupted upon thermal injury.
source: As previously reported (LeBert et al., 2018), collagen fibers were completely disrupted upon thermal injury but without the loss of the tissue, as measured by the area devoid of fibers (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and citation to prior work.

claim: Thermal injury did not result in loss of tissue.
source: As previously reported (LeBert et al., 2018), collagen fibers were completely disrupted upon thermal injury but without the loss of the tissue, as measured by the area devoid of fibers (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG microscopy and brightfield imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Collagen fibers began to reappear over time and were clearly visible by 72–96 hpw in burn wounds.
source: Collagen fibers began to reappear over time and were clearly visible by 72–96 hpw, extending progressively outward (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG microscopy data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The collagen fiber organization relative to the wound edge was comparable to the simple transection during repair in burn wounds.
source: Despite this initial disruption in collagen integrity, the collagen fiber organization relative to the wound edge was comparable to the simple transection during repair (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber angle measurements shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: The time line for the progression in collagen fiber reappearance coincides with the time period when healing recovers in the burn wound (72–96 hpw).
source: Interestingly, this time line for the progression in collagen fiber reappearance coincides, similarly as the shift in macrophage activation, with the time period when healing recovers in the burn wound (72–96 hpw; Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from temporal correlation between collagen fiber reappearance and healing recovery.

claim: Lm-infected transection showed limited damage to collagen fibers but disrupted tissue at the wound area early after wounding.
source: In the case of the Lm-infected transection we observed the opposite pattern: limited damage to collagen fibers but disrupted tissue at the wound area early after wounding (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG microscopy and brightfield imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Dysregulated collagen fiber organization became apparent over time in Lm-infected transection.
source: However, dysregulated collagen fiber organization became apparent over time as indicated by the increasing area devoid of collagen fibers (Figure 3A,D), as well as fibers becoming disarrayed and less perpendicular to the wound edge (Figure 3A,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG microscopy data showing increased area devoid of fibers and altered fiber angles in Figure 3A,D,E.

claim: The number of vimGFP-positive cells at the wound edge was similar between the simple transection and the burn wound.
source: The number of vimGFP-positive cells at the wound edge was similar between the simple transection and the burn wound, but markedly different in response to the Lm-infected transection (Figure 3F,G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by vimGFP-positive cell count data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: The number of vimGFP-positive cells progressively declined to nearly undetectable levels in the Lm-infected wound.
source: The number of vimGFP-positive cells progressively declined to nearly undetectable levels in the Lm-infected wound (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by vimGFP-positive cell count data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: Vimentin expression at the wound microenvironment recovers by 120 hpw in Lm-infected tail wounds.
source: Examination of the Lm-infected tail wound at later time points revealed that vimentin expression at the wound microenviroment recovers by 120 hpw (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by vimGFP imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Vimentin supports collagen fiber production and organization during wound repair.
source: These observations are consistent with, and extend, our previous findings that vimentin supports collagen fiber production and organization during wound repair (LeBert et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and data in the current manuscript.

claim: The absence of vimentin-expressing cells at the Lm-infected wound temporally correlates with a defect in collagen fiber remodeling accompanied by impaired wound repair.
source: The absence of vimGFP-positive cells at the Lm-infected wound temporally correlates with a defect in collagen fiber remodeling accompanied by impaired wound repair.
evidence: This claim is inferred from temporal correlation between loss of vimentin-expressing cells and impaired collagen remodeling/healing.

claim: The loss of vimentin-expressing cells at the wound edge in the presence of infection is likely due to combination of multiple factors, such as cell death and inflammation.
source: The loss of vimentin-expressing cells at the wound edge in the presence of infection was unexpected. This is likely due to combination of multiple factors, such as cell death and inflammation.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: Infection with hly mutant of L. monocytogenes failed to cause the loss and delay in the appearance of vimGFP-positive cells at the wound edge.
source: Interestingly, when we infected with the hly mutant of L. monocytogenes, a mutant that fails to escape from the phagosome and enter the cytosol of the host cell resulting in attenuated L. monocytogenes virulence (Theisen and Sauer, 2016), we failed to observe the loss and delay in the appearance of vimGFP-positive cells at the wound edge, while detecting drastically reduced inflammation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B) compared to wild-type L. monocytogenes infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data comparing wild-type and hly mutant L. monocytogenes infection shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The hly mutant of L. monocytogenes fails to escape from the phagosome and enter the cytosol of the host cell resulting in attenuated L. monocytogenes virulence.
source: Interestingly, when we infected with the hly mutant of L. monocytogenes, a mutant that fails to escape from the phagosome and enter the cytosol of the host cell resulting in attenuated L. monocytogenes virulence (Theisen and Sauer, 2016), we failed to observe the loss and delay in the appearance of vimGFP-positive cells at the wound edge, while detecting drastically reduced inflammation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B) compared to wild-type L. monocytogenes infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Theisen and Sauer, 2016).

claim: The excessive inflammation associated with Lm-infected tail wound may contribute to the loss and delay of the vimentin-expressing cells.
source: These findings indicate that the excessive inflammation associated with Lm-infected tail wound may contribute to the loss and delay of the vimentin-expressing cells, providing evidence that there is a crosstalk between the immune response and the presence of vimentin-expressing cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of wild-type and hly mutant L. monocytogenes infection effects.

claim: There is a crosstalk between the immune response and the presence of vimentin-expressing cells.
source: These findings indicate that the excessive inflammation associated with Lm-infected tail wound may contribute to the loss and delay of the vimentin-expressing cells, providing evidence that there is a crosstalk between the immune response and the presence of vimentin-expressing cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that reduced inflammation (hly mutant) preserves vimentin-expressing cells.

claim: STAT3 is a transcription factor reported to enhance the expression of the vimentin gene.
source: To begin identifying pathways that regulate the dynamics of vimentin-expressing cells at the wound microenvironment and their effects on repair, we examined the role of signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3), a transcription factor reported to enhance the expression of the vimentin gene (Wu et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Wu et al., 2004).

claim: Tissue regrowth at 72 hr post tail transection of stat3+/- larvae was similar to that of wild-type larvae.
source: Tissue regrowth at 72 hr post tail transection (hptt) of stat3stl27/+ (stat3+/-) larvae was similar to that of wild-type (stat3+/+) larvae, while it was significantly impaired in stat3stl27/stl27 (stat3-/-) larvae (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue regrowth area measurements shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Tissue regrowth at 72 hr post tail transection was significantly impaired in stat3-/- larvae.
source: Tissue regrowth at 72 hr post tail transection (hptt) of stat3stl27/+ (stat3+/-) larvae was similar to that of wild-type (stat3+/+) larvae, while it was significantly impaired in stat3stl27/stl27 (stat3-/-) larvae (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue regrowth area measurements shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The stat3 mutants were reported to exhibit normal development up to 15 dpf.
source: This defect is most likely wound-specific and not due to hindered development as the stat3 mutants were reported to exhibit normal development up to 15 dpf (Liu et al., 2017b), although we did detect a small reduction in tail fin area of age-matched unwounded larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Liu et al., 2017b).

claim: A small reduction in tail fin area of age-matched unwounded larvae was detected in stat3 mutants.
source: This defect is most likely wound-specific and not due to hindered development as the stat3 mutants were reported to exhibit normal development up to 15 dpf (Liu et al., 2017b), although we did detect a small reduction in tail fin area of age-matched unwounded larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by tail fin area measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The number of vimGFP-positive cells were reduced in the stat3 mutants compared to wild-type larvae at 72 hptt.
source: The number of vimGFP-positive cells were reduced in the stat3 mutants compared to wild-type larvae (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by vimGFP-positive cell count data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The vimGFP-positive cells at the wound did not arise early and then disappear by 72 hptt in stat3 mutants, as their numbers were also lower at 24 hptt.
source: The vimGFP-positive cells at the wound did not arise early and then disappear by 72 hptt, as their numbers were also lower at 24 hptt in the stat3 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by vimGFP-positive cell count data at 24 hptt shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Stat3 regulates the presence of vimentin-expressing cells specifically during wound responses.
source: These data suggest that Stat3 regulates the presence of vimentin-expressing cells specifically during wound responses, as vimGFP-expressing cells along the edge of the caudal fin of age-matched unwounded larvae appear unaffected in the stat3 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of wounded versus unwounded stat3 mutants shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The wound edge of the stat3 mutants was smoother and appeared to lack collagen-based projections.
source: Furthermore, the wound edge of the stat3 mutants was smoother and appeared to lack collagen-based projections (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by brightfield and SHG imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Collagen fibers failed to grow and exhibited less projections in the stat3 mutants.
source: Interestingly, while collagen fibers failed to grow and exhibited less projections in the stat3 mutants, they appeared to have normal organization (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Collagen fibers appeared to have normal organization in the stat3 mutants.
source: Interestingly, while collagen fibers failed to grow and exhibited less projections in the stat3 mutants, they appeared to have normal organization (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was a significant reduction in wound contour in the stat3 mutants, suggesting a reduction in projections.
source: We quantified projections at the wound edge by measuring the wound contour as previously (LeBert et al., 2018) and found a significant reduction in the stat3 mutants (Figure 4E), suggesting a reduction in projections.
evidence: This claim is supported by wound contour measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Vimentin was necessary for the formation of collagen-based projections at the wound edge.
source: This is consistent with our previous observations that vimentin was necessary for the formation of these collagen-based projections at the wound edge (LeBert et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (LeBert et al., 2018).

claim: TGFβ is known to be critical in wound healing and modulate STAT3 signaling.
source: In addition to Stat3, we examined the role of TGFβ in regulating wound-associated vimentin-expressing cells, as TGFβ is known to be critical in wound healing and modulate STAT3 signaling (Aztekin et al., 2019; Derynck and Budi, 2019; Lichtman et al., 2016; Pakyari et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on TGFβ function.

claim: Disrupting the TGFβ pathway leads to impaired tissue regrowth following tail transection.
source: Using ALK5/TGFβ receptor I inhibitor, we found that disrupting the TGFβ pathway leads to impaired tissue regrowth and significantly diminished number of vimGFP-positive cells at the wound edge following tail transection (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue regrowth area measurements with ALK5 inhibitor shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: Disrupting the TGFβ pathway leads to significantly diminished number of vimGFP-positive cells at the wound edge following tail transection.
source: Using ALK5/TGFβ receptor I inhibitor, we found that disrupting the TGFβ pathway leads to impaired tissue regrowth and significantly diminished number of vimGFP-positive cells at the wound edge following tail transection (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by vimGFP-positive cell count data with ALK5 inhibitor shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: The effect of TGFβ inhibition appears to be wound-specific, as the tail fin area and vimGFP-positive cells in age-matched unwounded control appear normal.
source: This outcome appears to be wound-specific, as the tail fin area and vimGFP-positive cells in age-matched unwounded control appear normal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from unwounded larvae treated with ALK5 inhibitor shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: TGFβ is known to modulate STAT3 signaling.
source: Since TGFβ is known to modulate STAT3 signaling (Derynck and Budi, 2019), in future studies we plan to examine whether TGFβ regulates the dynamics of wound-associated vimentin-expressing cells via Stat3.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Derynck and Budi, 2019).

claim: Diminishing vimentin-expressing cells at the wound edge either by infection, or disrupting Stat3 or TGFβ pathways leads to impaired wound healing.
source: Our collective observations, that diminishing vimentin-expressing cells at the wound edge either by infection, or disrupting Stat3 or TGFβ pathways leads to impaired wound healing, support the idea that wound-associated vimentin-expressing cells are necessary for proper wound healing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective observations across different experimental conditions.

claim: Wound-associated vimentin-expressing cells are necessary for proper wound healing.
source: Our collective observations, that diminishing vimentin-expressing cells at the wound edge either by infection, or disrupting Stat3 or TGFβ pathways leads to impaired wound healing, support the idea that wound-associated vimentin-expressing cells are necessary for proper wound healing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between vimentin-expressing cells and wound healing outcomes.

claim: The burn wound was associated with an intermediate inflammatory response compared to tail transection.
source: The burn wound was associated with an intermediate inflammatory response, loss of collagen fibers with no effect on vimGFP-positive cells, and delayed healing as compared to tail transection.
evidence: This claim is supported by leukocyte recruitment data showing higher inflammation than transection but lower than infection.

claim: The burn wound showed loss of collagen fibers with no effect on vimGFP-positive cells.
source: The burn wound was associated with an intermediate inflammatory response, loss of collagen fibers with no effect on vimGFP-positive cells, and delayed healing as compared to tail transection.
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG microscopy and vimentin reporter data.

claim: The burn wound showed delayed healing as compared to tail transection.
source: The burn wound was associated with an intermediate inflammatory response, loss of collagen fibers with no effect on vimGFP-positive cells, and delayed healing as compared to tail transection.
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue regrowth area measurements.

claim: The infected wound had the least regenerative capacity with the most extensive inflammation and tissue damage.
source: The infected wound had the least regenerative capacity with the most extensive inflammation and tissue damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue regrowth and leukocyte recruitment data.

claim: The loss of vimGFP-positive cells and impaired collagen reorganization correlated with the defect in repair in infected wounds.
source: Most striking was the loss of vimGFP-positive cells and impaired collagen reorganization that correlated with the defect in repair.
evidence: This claim is inferred from temporal correlation between loss of vimentin-expressing cells, collagen disorganization, and impaired healing.

claim: Disrupting either Stat3 or TGFβ pathway leads to diminished numbers of vimentin-expressing cells at the wound site accompanied by impaired healing.
source: In addition, we identified Stat3 and TGFβ as important signaling pathways in regulating the dynamics of vimentin-expressing cells during wound response, since disrupting either pathway leads to diminished numbers of vimentin-expressing cells at the wound site accompanied by impaired healing.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from stat3 mutants and TGFβ inhibitor experiments.

claim: The wound models presented expand the toolkit to study tissue healing and regeneration.
source: Collectively, the wound models presented here expand our toolkit to study tissue healing and regeneration, and provide a useful in vivo approach to investigate mechanisms of crosstalk between the innate immune system and the remodeling machinery in response to complex injuries.
evidence: This claim is based on the characterization of new wound models in the manuscript.
